āgatam api taṃ savidhe paricayahīneva vīkṣate bālā//"
atra kāntaviyogo vibhāvaḥ/ indriyavaikalyaṃ lajjādyabhāvaś cānubhāvaḥ/
yathā vā--
"śuṇḍādaṇḍaṃ kuṇḍalīkṛtya kūle kallolinyāḥ kiṃcid ākuñcitākṣaḥ/
naivākarṣaty ambu naivāmbujāliṃ kāntāpetaḥ kṛtyaśūnyo gajendraḥ//"
body.translated_text:
"It is variegated by alternation with other states"—thus say the modern [scholars].
An example—
"With heart distracted by separation, lamenting 'O beloved, O beloved!', even when he has come near, the young woman looks at him as if without recognition." //
Here, separation from the lover is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The impairment of the senses and absence of shame and such are the <s>anubhāvas</s>.
Or, for example—
"Having coiled his trunk on the bank of the river of waves, with eyes slightly contracted, the great elephant, separated from his beloved, neither draws water nor [plucks] the lotus clusters, bereft of purpose." //

body.text: lobhaśokabhayādijanitopaplavanivāraṇakāraṇībhūtaś cittavṛttiviśeṣo dhṛtiḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Dhṛti</s> (fortitude) is a particular mental state that serves as the cause for warding off agitations produced by greed, sorrow, fear, and the like. //

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"saṃtāpayāmi hṛdayaṃ dhāvaṃ dhāvaṃ dharātale kim aham/
asti mama
śirasi satataṃ nandakumāraḥ prabhuḥ paramaḥ//"
atra vivekaśrutasaṃpattyādir vibhāvaḥ/ cāpalādyupaśamo 'nubhāvaḥ/ nanu cottarārdhe cintā nāstīti vastuno 'bhivyakteḥ katham asya dhṛtibhāvadhvanitvam iti cet, tasya dhṛtyupayogitayaivābhivyakteḥ/
body.translated_text:
An example—
"Why do I torment my heart, running and running upon the earth? The prince of <s>Nanda</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>), the supreme lord, is always upon my head!" //
Here, discrimination (<s>viveka</s>), listening to scripture (<s>śruta</s>), prosperity (<s>saṃpatti</s>), and the like are the <s>vibhāvas</s>. The subsiding of fickleness and such is the <s>anubhāva</s>. If one objects: 'In the latter half, what is manifested is the factual truth that anxiety does not exist—how then can this be <s>dhvani</s> of the <s>bhāva</s> of <s>dhṛti</s>?'—[the answer is:] because that truth is manifested precisely in its capacity of being useful for <s>dhṛti</s>.

body.text: kim aniṣṭaṃ mama bhaviṣyatīty ākāraś cittavṛttiviśeṣaḥ śaṅkā//
body.translated_text: <s>Śaṅkā</s> (apprehension) is a particular mental state of the form 'What misfortune will befall me?' //

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"vidhivañcitayā mayā na yātaṃ sakhi saṃketaniketanaṃ priyasya/
adhunā bata kiṃ vidhātukāmo mayi kāmo nṛpatiḥ punar na jāne//"
atra rājāparādho vibhāvaḥ/ mukhavaivarṇyādaya ākṣepyā anubhāvāḥ/ iyaṃ tu bhayādyutpādanena kampādikāriṇī, na tu cintā/
body.translated_text:
An example—
"Cheated by fate, I did not go, O friend, to the trysting-place of my beloved; now, alas, what does <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love), that king, intend to do with me? I do not know." //
Here, the offense against the king is the <s>vibhāva</s>. Pallor of the face and such are the implied <s>anubhāvas</s>. This [apprehension], however, by producing fear and such, causes trembling and the like—it is not mere <s>cintā</s> (anxiety).

body.text: ādhivyādhijanyabalahāniprabhavo vaivarṇyaśithilāṅgatvadṛgbhramaṇādihetur duḥkhaviśeṣo glāniḥ/
body.translated_text: <s>Glāni</s> (languor) is a particular form of suffering originating from loss of strength produced by mental and physical ailments (<s>ādhi</s> and <s>vyādhi</s>), which causes pallor, limpness of limbs, rolling of the eyes, and similar [symptoms].

body.text:
yathā--
"śayitā śaivalaśayane suṣamāśeṣā navendulekheva/
priyam āgatam api savidhe satkurute madhuravīkṣaṇair eva//"
atra priyaviraho vibhāvaḥ/ madhuravīkṣaṇair evety evakāreṇa bodhyamānā pratyudgamacaraṇanipatanāśleṣādīnāṃ nivṛttir anubhāvaḥ/ na cātra śramaḥ śaṅkyaḥ, kāraṇābhāvāt/ kecit tu vyādhyādiprabhavabalanāśaṃ glānim āhuḥ/ teṣāṃ mate cittavṛttyātmakeṣu bhāveṣu nāśarūpāyā glāneḥ kathaṃ samāveśa iti dhyeyam/ yady api "balasyāpacayo glānir ādhivyādhisamudbhavaḥ" iti lakṣaṇavākyād apacayaśabdena nāśa eva pratiyate, tathāpi prāg uktānupapattyā balanāśajanyaṃ duḥkham eva balāpacayaśabdena
vivakṣitam/
body.translated_text:
For example—
"Lying on a bed of moss, with only traces of her former beauty remaining, like a new crescent moon, even when her beloved has come near, she honors him only with sweet glances." //
Here, separation from the beloved is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The word 'only' (<s>eva</s>) indicates the absence of rising to greet him, falling at his feet, embracing, and such—this is the <s>anubhāva</s>. Here, <s>śrama</s> (fatigue) should not be suspected, due to the absence of [its] cause. Some, however, say <s>glāni</s> is the destruction of strength arising from illness and the like. In their view, one should consider how <s>glāni</s>, which is of the nature of destruction, can be included among the <s>bhāvas</s>, which are mental states. Although from the definitional statement 'Decline of strength is <s>glāni</s>, arising from mental and physical ailments,' the word 'decline' (<s>apacaya</s>) conveys destruction, nevertheless, due to the difficulty stated above, what is intended by the term 'decline of strength' is the suffering born from the loss of strength.

body.text: duḥkhadāridryāparādhādijanitaḥ svāpakarṣabhāṣaṇādihetuś cittavṛttiviśeṣo dainyam//
body.translated_text: <s>Dainya</s> (despondency) is a particular mental state produced by suffering, poverty, offenses, and the like, which causes self-deprecation in speech and similar [behaviors]. //

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"hatakena mayā vanāntare vanajākṣī sahasā vivāsitā/
adhunā mama kutra sā satī patitasyeva parā sarasvatī//"
sītāṃ parityaktavato bhagavataḥ śrīrāmabhadrasyeyam uktiḥ/ atra sītāparityāgarūpo 'parādhas tajjanyaṃ duḥkhaṃ vā vibhāvaḥ/ patitasāmyarūpasvāpakarṣabhāṣaṇam anubhāvaḥ/
yad āhuḥ--
"cintautsukyān manastāpād daurgatyāc ca vibhāvataḥ/
anubhāvāt tu śiraso 'bhyāvṛtter gātragauravāt//
body.translated_text:
An example—
"By me, a wretch, the lotus-eyed one was suddenly banished to the forest; now where is that virtuous woman for me—like higher learning for a fallen one?" //
This is the utterance of the blessed <s>Śrī Rāmabhadra</s> (<s>Rāma</s>) who had abandoned <s>Sītā</s>. Here, the offense in the form of abandoning <s>Sītā</s>, or the suffering born from it, is the <s>vibhāva</s>. Self-deprecation in the form of comparing oneself to a fallen one (<s>patita</s>) is the <s>anubhāva</s>.
As they state—
"From anxiety, eagerness, mental anguish, and misfortune as <s>vibhāvas</s>; and from <s>anubhāvas</s> such as covering of the head, heaviness of limbs, //

body.text:
dehopaskaraṇatyāgād dainyaṃ bhāvaṃ vibhāvayet//" iti/
"daurgatyāder anaujasyaṃ dainyaṃ malinatādikṛt/" iti ca/
atra hatakena mayā vivāsitā na tu vidhinety etasyārthasya patitopamayaiva paripoṣaḥ, na tu śūdrādyupamayā/ yataḥ śūdrasya jātyaiva śrutidaurlabhyaṃ vidhinā kṛtam/ patitasya tu brāhmaṇāder vidhinā śrutisulabhatve svabhāvena kṛte 'pi tenaiva tathāvidhaṃ pāpam ācaratā svataḥ śrutir dūrīkṛteti tasya patitena sāmyam, tasyāś ca śrutyety upamālaṃkāro dainyam evālaṃkurute/ tathā mayeti seti copādānalakṣaṇāmūladhvanibhyāṃ kṛtaghnatvakṛtajñātvanirdayatvadayāvatītvādyanekadharmaprakāśanadvārā tad eva paripoṣyate, seti smṛtyā ca leśataḥ pratīyamānayā/
body.translated_text:
abandonment of bodily adornment—one should recognize the <s>bhāva</s> of <s>dainya</s> (despondency)." //
"From misfortune and such, lack of vigor—<s>dainya</s> causes dirtiness and the like." //
Here, the meaning of 'By me, a wretch, she was banished—not by fate' is nourished precisely by the simile of the <s>patita</s> (fallen one), not by a simile with a <s>Śūdra</s> or the like. For a <s>Śūdra</s>'s difficulty in accessing scripture is created by fate through his very birth-caste. But for a fallen <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> and the like, even though fate has made scripture naturally accessible, he himself, by committing such sin, has distanced himself from scripture—hence his likeness to the fallen one, and hers to scripture. Thus the <s>upamā</s> (simile) figure adorns <s>dainya</s> itself. Furthermore, through the word-suggestions (<s>dhvani</s>) based on the figures of <s>upādāna</s> (synecdoche) in the words 'by me' and 'she,' the manifold qualities of ingratitude and gratitude, cruelty and compassion are revealed, thereby nourishing that very [<s>dainya</s>]; and the <s>smṛti</s> (memory) [of <s>Sītā</s>], perceived in a slight degree [through the word 'she'], also [nourishes it].

body.text: iṣṭāprāptyaniṣṭaprāptyādijanitā dhyānāparaparyāyā vaivarṇyabhūlekhanādhomukhatvādihetuś cittavṛttiviśeṣaś cintā//
body.translated_text: <s>Cintā</s> (anxiety) is a particular mental state, synonymous with <s>dhyāna</s> (brooding), born from non-attainment of the desired, attainment of the undesired, and the like, which causes pallor, drawing on the ground, downcast face, and similar [behaviors]. //

body.text:
yad āhuḥ--
"vibhāvā yatra dāridryam aiśvaryabhraṃśanaṃ tathā/
iṣṭārthāpahṛtiḥ śaśvacchvāsocchvāsāv adhomukham//
body.translated_text:
As they state—
"The <s>vibhāvas</s> in this case are poverty, loss of prosperity, deprivation of desired objects; constant sighing, downcast face, //

body.text:
saṃtāpaḥ smaraṇaṃ caiva kārśyaṃ dehānupaskṛtiḥ/
adhṛtiś cānubhāvāḥ syuḥ sā cintā parikīrtitā//
body.translated_text: anguish, remembering, emaciation, neglect of bodily appearance, and lack of composure—these are the <s>anubhāvas</s>; that is declared to be <s>cintā</s> (anxiety). //

body.text:
vitarko 'syāḥ kṣaṇe pūrve pāścāttye vopajāyate//" iti/
"dhyānaṃ cintā hitānāpteḥ saṃtāpādikarī matā/" iti ca/
udāharaṇam-
"adharadyutir astapallavā mukhaśobhā śaśikāntilaṅghinī/
akṛtapratimā tanuḥ kṛtā vidhinā kasya kṛte mṛgīdṛśaḥ//"
atra tadaprāptir vibhāvaḥ/ anutāpādaya ākṣepyā anubhāvāḥ/ na cātrautsukyadhvanir iti vācyam/ kasya kṛtaity anirdhāritadharmyālambanāyāś cintāyā eva pratīyamānatayā sato 'py autsukyasyaitadvākyena prādhānyenā 'bodhanāt/
body.translated_text:
Deliberation (<s>vitarka</s>) about her arises in the preceding or the following moment."
"Thought (<s>dhyāna</s>) is <s>cintā</s> (anxious contemplation), which, due to the non-attainment of what is desired, is considered as causing distress and the like."
Example:
"The luster of her lip surpasses tender shoots, her facial beauty eclipses the splendor of the moon; matchless is the body of the doe-eyed one fashioned by the Creator — for whose sake?"
Here the non-attainment of her is the <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant). Remorse and the like, which are to be inferred, are the <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents). And one should not say that here there is suggestion of eagerness (<s>autsukya</s>) — because through the expression 'for whose sake,' it is <s>cintā</s> (thought) directed toward an <s>ālambana</s> (object) whose possessor is undetermined that is perceived as primary, and although eagerness exists, it is not principally conveyed by this expression.

body.text: madyādyupayogajanmā ullāsākhyaḥ śayanahasitādihetuś cittavṛttiviśeṣo madaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Mada</s> (intoxication) is a particular mental state (<s>cittavṛttiviśeṣa</s>) born from the consumption of liquor and the like, called elation (<s>ullāsa</s>), which is the cause of lying down, laughter, and the like. //

body.text:
yadāhuḥ--
"saṃmohānandasaṃdoho mado madyopayogajaḥ/" iti/ tatrottame puruṣe svāpo 'nubhāvaḥ/ madhyame hasitagāne/ nīce tu rodanaparuṣoktyādi/ ayaṃ madas trividhaḥ, taruṇamadhyamādhamabhedāt/ avyaktāsaṃgatavākyaiḥ sukumāraskhaladgatyā ca yo 'bhinīyate sa ādyāḥ/ bhujākṣepaskhalitaghūrṇitādibhir madhyamaḥ/ gatibhaṅgasmṛtināśahikkācchardyābhir adhamaḥ/
body.translated_text:
As they say:
"<s>Mada</s>, born from the use of liquor, is an assemblage of delusion and bliss."
Therein, in the highest person, sleep is the <s>anubhāva</s> (consequent). In the middling, laughter and singing. In the lowest, weeping, harsh speech, etc. This <s>mada</s> is threefold, by the division into mild (<s>taruṇa</s>), moderate (<s>madhyama</s>), and severe (<s>adhama</s>). That which is enacted with indistinct, incoherent utterances and a delicate, stumbling gait is the first [mild]. The moderate [is enacted] with flailing arms, stumbling, swaying, etc. The severe [is enacted] with breakdown of gait, loss of memory, hiccups, and vomiting.

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"madhurataraṃ smayamānaḥ svasminn evālapañ śanaiḥ kim api/
kokanadayaṃs trilokīm ālambanaśūnyam īkṣate kṣībaḥ//"
atra mādakadravyasevanaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ avyaktālāpādy anubhāvaḥ/ atra mattasvabhāvavarṇanasya tanniṣṭhamadavyañjanārthatvān madabhāva eva pradhānam iti na svabhāvoktyalaṃkārasyaprādhānyam, api tu taddhvanyupaskārakatvam eva/
idaṃ vā punar udāharaṇam--
"madhurasān madhuraṃ hi tavādharaṃ taruṇi madvadane viniveśaya/
mama gṛhāṇa kareṇa karāmbujaṃ papapatāmi hahā bhabhabhūtale//"
atrāpi sa eva vibhāvaḥ/ adhikavarṇoccāraṇādir anubhāvaḥ/ pūrvārdhagatā grāmyoktir uttarārdhe ca taruṇīkare 'mbujopameyatayā nirūpaṇīye svakarasya tadupameyatayā nirūpaṇaṃ ca madam eva poṣayataḥ/
body.translated_text:
Example:
"Smiling most sweetly, murmuring softly something to himself, compassionating the triple world — the intoxicated one (<s>kṣība</s>) gazes without any object [of focus]."
Here the consumption of an intoxicating substance is the <s>vibhāva</s>. Indistinct prattling etc. are the <s>anubhāvas</s>. Here, since the description of the nature of the intoxicated person serves the purpose of suggesting the <s>mada</s> (intoxication) residing in him, it is the <s>bhāva</s> of <s>mada</s> itself that is primary — not the figure of <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description); rather, [the description] serves merely as an enhancer of that suggestion.
Or this other example:
"O young woman, place your sweet lip, which tastes sweeter still, upon my face! Take my lotus-hand with your hand! I'm fa-fa-falling, ha-ha, on the gro-gro-ground!"
Here too the same <s>vibhāva</s> [applies]. The reduplicated pronunciation of syllables etc. is the <s>anubhāva</s>. The vulgar speech in the first half, and in the second half the description of one's own hand as the object of lotus-comparison when it is the young woman's hand that should be so compared — both nourish the <s>mada</s> alone.

body.text: bahutaraśārīravyāpārajanmā niḥśvā sāṅgasaṃmardanidrādikāraṇībhūtaḥ khedaviśeṣaḥ śramaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Śrama</s> (fatigue) is a particular kind of weariness (<s>khedaviśeṣa</s>), born from excessive bodily exertion, which becomes the cause of sighing, massage of the limbs, sleep, and the like. //

body.text:
yad ahuḥ--
"adhvavyāyāmasevādyair vibhāvair anubhāvakaiḥ/
gātrasaṃvāhanair āsya saṃkocair aṅgamoṭanaiḥ//
body.translated_text:
As they say:
"With <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) such as travel, exercise, exertion, and the like; with <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents) such as massage of the limbs, contraction of the face, stretching of the body,

body.text:
niḥśvāsairjṛmbhitair mandaiḥ pādotkṣepaiḥ śramo mataḥ//" iti/
"śramaḥ khedo 'dhvagatyāder nidrāśvāsādikṛnmataḥ/" iti ca/
ayaṃ ca saty api bale jāyate, śārīravyāpārād eva ca jāyate, na tu glāniḥ/ ato glāneḥ śramasya bhedaḥ/
udāharaṇam--
"vidhāya sā madvadanānukūlaṃ kapolamūlaṃ hṛdaye śayānā/
cirāya citre likhiteva tanvī na spandituṃ mandam api kṣamāsīt//"
atra viparītasuratarūpaḥ śārīravyāpāro vibhāvaḥ/ spandarāhityaśayanādayo 'nubhāvāḥ/ na cātra nidrābhāvadhvananena gatārthateti śaṅkyam/ suṣuptau hi jñānarāhityenaiva yatnarāhityān mandam api spandituṃ na kṣamāsīd ity asyānatiprayojanakatvāpatteḥ, śīṅābhihitatayā tasyā vyaṅgyatvānupapatteś ca/ śrame tv ānuguṇyam ucitam/
body.translated_text:
Sighing, yawning, slowness, and lifting of the feet — [this] is considered <s>śrama</s> (fatigue)."
"<s>Śrama</s> is weariness from traveling and the like, considered as causing sleep, sighing, etc."
And this arises even when strength is present, and arises from bodily exertion alone — but <s>glāni</s> (languor) [arises differently]. Hence the distinction of <s>śrama</s> from <s>glāni</s>.
Example:
"Having placed her cheek-base turned toward my face, lying upon [my] heart, the slender one, as if painted in a picture, was unable to stir even slightly for a long time."
Here the bodily exertion in the form of <s>viparīta-surata</s> (inverted love-making) is the <s>vibhāva</s>. Absence of movement, lying down, etc. are the <s>anubhāvas</s>. And one should not suspect that this is accounted for by the suggestion of the <s>bhāva</s> of sleep (<s>nidrā</s>) — for in deep sleep, due to the absence of cognition leading to absence of effort, the expression 'was unable to stir even slightly' would be practically purposeless; and because sleep, being stated by the verbal root '<s>śīṅ</s>' (to lie), its being suggested is untenable. But in fatigue, the propriety is fitting.

body.text: rūpadhanavidyādipratyuktātmotkarṣajñānādhīnaparāvahelanaṃ garvaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Garva</s> (pride) is the disdain of others dependent on the knowledge of one's own superiority confirmed in beauty, wealth, learning, and the like. //

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"ā mūlād ratnasānor malayavalayitād ā ca kūlāt payodher
yāvantaḥ santi kāvyapraṇayanapaṭavas te viśaṅkaṃ vadantu/
mṛdvīkāmadhyaniryanmasṛṇarasajharīmādhurībhāgyabhājāṃ
vācām ācāryatāyāḥ padam anubhavituṃ ko 'sti dhanyo madanyaḥ//"
atra svakīyakavitāyā ananyasādhāraṇatājñānaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ parādhikṣepaparaitādṛśavākyaprayogo 'nubhāvaḥ/ imaṃ cāsūyāpi leśataḥ puṣṇāti/ utsāhapradhāno gūḍhagarvo hi vīrarasadhvaniḥ, ayaṃ tu garvapradhāna iti tasmād asya viśeṣaḥ/ tathā hi vīrarasaprasaṅge prāg udāhṛte "yadi vakti-"ityādi padye gīṣpatināgirām adhidevatayāpi sākam ahaṃ vadiṣyāmīti vacanenābhivyaktasyotsāhasya paripoṣakatayā sthitaḥ sarvebhyaḥ paṇḍitebhyo 'ham adhika iti garvaḥ, na tu prakṛtapadya iva nāsty eva mahītale madanya iti sphuṭoditena solluṇṭhavacanenānubhāvena prādhānyena pratīyamānaḥ/
body.translated_text:
Example:
"From the base of the jeweled mountain [<s>Meru</s>], encircled by [the] <s>Malaya</s>, to the shores of the ocean — let all who are skilled in the composition of poetry speak without hesitation! Who other than I is so fortunate as to attain the mastery over speech that partakes of the sweetness of the smooth stream of juice flowing from within ripe grapes?"
Here the knowledge of the unparalleled nature of one's own poetry is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The use of such speech aimed at reproaching others is the <s>anubhāva</s>. Even a trace of envy (<s>asūyā</s>) nourishes this. For the <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) of <s>vīra-rasa</s> (heroic sentiment) has enthusiasm (<s>utsāha</s>) as primary and pride as concealed; but this [example] has pride as primary — hence its distinction from that. Thus, in the <s>vīra-rasa</s> passage previously cited, in the verse 'yadi vakti-' etc., the pride 'I am superior to all <s>paṇḍitas</s>' stands as nourishing the enthusiasm that is manifested by the statement 'I shall argue even with <s>Gīṣpati</s> (<s>Bṛhaspati</s>), the lord of divine speech'; but it is not, as in the present verse, perceived primarily through a bold utterance such as 'there is no one on earth other than me' stated as an <s>anubhāva</s> (consequent).

body.text: śramādiprayojyaṃ cetaḥsaṃmīlanaṃ nidrā//
body.translated_text: <s>Nidrā</s> (sleep) is the closing of the mind brought about by fatigue and the like. //

body.text:
netranimīlanagātraniṣkriyatvādayo 'syā anubhāvāḥ/
udāharaṇam--
"sā madāgamanabṛṃhitatoṣā jāgareṇa gamitākhiladoṣā/
bodhitāpi bubudhe madhūpair na prātar ānanajasaurabhalubdhaiḥ//"
rātrijāgaraṇaśramo 'tra vibhāvaḥ/ madhupair bodhābhāvo 'nubhāvaḥ/
body.translated_text:
Closing of the eyes, inactivity of the body, and the like are its <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents).
Example:
"She, whose joy was nourished by the coming of her beloved, whose every fault had been dispelled by her vigil — even when awakened in the morning by bees greedy for the fragrance of her mouth, she did not wake up."
Here the fatigue from staying awake at night is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The failure to be awakened by the bees is the <s>anubhāva</s>.

body.text: śāstrādivicārajanyam arthanirdhāraṇaṃ matiḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Mati</s> (deliberation) is the determination of meaning born from reflection on treatises (<s>śāstra</s>) and the like. //

body.text:
atra niḥśaṅkatadarthānuṣṭhānasaṃśayocchedādayo 'nubhāvāḥ/
udāharaṇam--
"nikhilaṃ jagad eva naśvaraṃ punar asmin nitarāṃ kalevaram/
atha tasya kṛte kiyānayaṃ kriyate hanta mayā pariśramaḥ//"
"śarīram etajjalabudbudopamam" ityādiśāstraparyālocanam atra vibhāvaḥ/ hantapadagamyā svanindā rājasevādiviratir vitṛṣṇatā cānubhāvaḥ/ jhagiti mater eva camatkārād dhvanivyapadeśahetutā, na śāntasya, vilambena pratiteḥ/
body.translated_text:
Here, fearless adherence to that meaning, resolution of doubt, etc. are the <s>anubhāvas</s>.
Example:
"Indeed the entire world is perishable; and among things in it, the body most of all. So for the sake of that [body], how much effort, alas, am I exerting?"
The contemplation of treatises such as 'This body is comparable to a water-bubble' etc. is the <s>vibhāva</s> here. Self-reproach conveyed by the word 'alas' (<s>hanta</s>), cessation from service of kings etc., and dispassion are the <s>anubhāvas</s>. Because of the immediate aesthetic delight (<s>camatkāra</s>) from <s>mati</s> (deliberation) itself, it is the ground for the designation of <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) — not <s>śānta-rasa</s> (tranquil sentiment), since that is perceived only with delay.

body.text: rogavirahādiprabhavo manastāpo vyādhiḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Vyādhi</s> (disease) is mental distress arising from illness, separation, and the like. //

body.text:
gātraśaithilyaśvāsādayo 'trānubhāvāḥ/
yadāhuḥ--
"ekaikaśo dvandvaśo vā trayāṇāṃ vā prakopataḥ/
vātapittakaphānāṃ syur vyādhayo ye jvarādayaḥ//
body.translated_text:
Looseness of limbs, heavy breathing, and the like are its <s>anubhāvas</s> here.
As they say:
"Diseases such as fever and others arise from the disturbance of <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>kapha</s> (phlegm), singly, in pairs, or all three together.

body.text:
iha tatprabhavo bhāvo vyādhir ity abhidhīyate//"
udāharaṇam--
"hṛdaye kṛtaśaivalānuṣaṅgā muhur aṅgāni yatas tataḥ kṣipantī/
tadudantapare mukhe sakhīnām atidīnām iyam ādadhāti dṛṣṭim//"
viraho 'tra vibhāvaḥ/ aṅgakṣepādir anubhāvaḥ/
body.translated_text:
Here, the emotion (<s>bhāva</s>) arising from that [disturbance] is called <s>vyādhi</s> (disease)."
Example:
"With moss-like [discolorations] clinging to her heart, repeatedly tossing her limbs this way and that — this [woman], exceedingly wretched, casts her gaze upon the faces of her friends who are anxious about his news."
Here separation is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The tossing of limbs etc. is the <s>anubhāva</s>.

body.text: bhīror ghorasattvadarśanasphūrjathuśravaṇādijanmā cittavṛttiviśeṣas trāsaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Trāsa</s> (terror) is a particular mental state of a timid person, born from seeing fearsome creatures, hearing thunder, and the like. //

body.text:
anubhāvāś cāsya romāñcakampastambhabhramādayaḥ/
yadāhuḥ--
"autpātikair manaḥ kṣepas trāsaḥ kampādikārakaḥ/"
udāharaṇam--
"ālīṣu kelīrabhasena bālā muhur mamālāpam upālapantī/"
ārād upākarṇya giraṃ madīyāṃ saudāminīyāṃ suṣamā mayāsīt//
body.translated_text:
And its <s>anubhāvas</s> are horripilation, trembling, paralysis, bewilderment, etc.
As they say: "<s>Trāsa</s> is the agitation of mind caused by portentous events, producing trembling and the like."
Example:
"The young girl, who was repeatedly mimicking my speech in the rush of playfulness among her friends — upon hearing my voice from afar, became like a streak of lightning [i.e., vanished in a flash]."

body.text:
atra patyā svavacanākarṇanaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ palāyanam anubhāvaḥ/ na cātra lajjāyā vyaṅgyatvam āśaṅkanīyam/ śaiśavenaiva tasyā nirāsāt/
idaṃ vā viviktam udāharaṇam--
"mā
kuru kaśāṃ karābje karuṇāvati kampate mama svāntam/
khelan na jātu gopair amba vilambaṃ kariṣyāmi//"
eṣā bhagavato līlāgopakiśorasyoktiḥ/
body.translated_text:
Here the hearing of her own words [being mimicked] by her husband is the <s>vibhāva</s>. Flight is the <s>anubhāva</s>. And one should not suspect that modesty (<s>lajjā</s>) is what is suggested here, since it is precluded by her very childishness.
Or this clearer example:
"Do not take the whip in your lotus-hand, O compassionate mother! My heart trembles! Never again while playing with the cowherd boys will I be late, O mother!"
This is the speech of the Lord in his divine play as a young cowherd boy (<s>līlā-gopa-kiśora</s>).

body.text: nidrāvibhāvotthajñānaṃ suptam//
body.translated_text: <s>Supta</s> (dreaming) is the cognition arising from sleep as its <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant). //

body.text:
svapna iti yāvat/ asyānubhāvaḥ pralāpādiḥ/ netranimīlanādayas tu nidrāyā evānubhāvā na tv asya, anidaṃjanyatvāt/ yat tu prācīnaiḥ "asyānubhāvā nibhṛtagātranetranimīlanaṃ" ityādy uktaṃ tadanyathāsiddhānām api teṣām etadbhāvavyāpakatvād iti dhyeyam/
udāharaṇam--
"akaruṇa mṛṣābhāṣāsindho vimuñca mamāñcalaṃ
tava paricitaḥ snehaḥ samyaṅ mayety anubhāṣiṇīm/
aviralagaladbāṣpāṃ tanvīṃ nirastavibhūṣaṇāṃ
ka iha bhavatīṃ bhadre nidre vinā vinivedayet//"
eṣā pravāsagatasya svapne 'pi priyām evaṃbhāṣiṇīṃ dṛṣṭavato nidrāṃ prati kasyacid uktiḥ/ yady apy evaṃbhūtāyāḥ priyatamāvasthāyā nivedanena nidre mama bhavatyā mahānupakāraḥ kṛta iti vastu, vipralambhaśṛṅgāraś cātra pratītipatham avatarati, tathāpi puraḥsphūrtikatayā svapnadhvananam atrodāhṛtaṃ, na prānte tayor dhvananaṃ niroddhum īṣṭe/
body.translated_text:
That is, dream (<s>svapna</s>). Its <s>anubhāva</s> is delirious speech (<s>pralāpa</s>) and the like. But closing of the eyes etc. are <s>anubhāvas</s> of sleep (<s>nidrā</s>) alone, not of this [dreaming], since they are not produced by it. As for what the ancients stated — 'its <s>anubhāvas</s> are stillness of body, closing of eyes' etc. — this should be considered [correct] because even though those [signs] are established otherwise [i.e., as signs of sleep], they pervade this <s>bhāva</s> [of dreaming as well].
Example:
"'O merciless one, O ocean of false speeches, release my garment-hem! Your affection for me is well known to me' — so she was replying. With tears flowing incessantly, the slender one, her ornaments cast aside — O good <s>Nidrā</s> (Sleep), who in this world other than you could have revealed her thus?"
This is the address to <s>Nidrā</s> (Sleep) by one who, gone to a distant land, saw his beloved speaking thus even in a dream. Although the content (<s>vastu</s>) is that 'O <s>Nidrā</s>, you have done me a great favor by revealing my beloved in this state,' and although <s>vipralambha-śṛṅgāra</s> (love-in-separation) too enters the path of perception here, nevertheless, because the dreaming [state] comes to the foreground, the suggestion of dream is what is illustrated here — it is not possible to suppress the suggestion of those two [vastu and vipralambha] at the end.

body.text: nidrānāśottaraṃ jāyamāno bodho vibodhaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Vibodha</s> (waking) is the consciousness that arises after the cessation of sleep. //

body.text:
nidrānāśaś ca tatpūrtisvapnāntabalavacchabdasparśādibhir jāyata iti ta evātra vibhāvāḥ/ akṣimardanagātramardanādayo 'nubhāvāḥ/
tatra
saṃkṣepeṇodāharaṇam--
"nitarāṃ hitayādya nidrayā me bata yāme carame niveditāyāḥ/
sudṛśo vacanaṃ śṛṇomi yāvan mayi tāvat pracukopa vārivāhaḥ//"
atra garjitaśravaṇaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ priyāvacanaśravaṇollāsanāśo 'nubhāvas tūnneyaḥ/ kecid avidyādhvaṃsajanyam apy amum āmananti/ teṣāṃ mate--
"naṣṭo mohaḥ smṛtir labdhā tvatprasādān mayācyuta/
sthito 'smi gatasaṃdehaḥ kariṣye vacanaṃ tava//"
iti gītāpadyam udāhāryam/ na tu vārivāhaviṣayāyā asūyāyā evātra vākyārthateti śaṅkyam/ vibodhapratītau hi satyāṃ tasminn anaucityāvagame saty anucitavibodhajanakatvena vārivāhe 'sūyāyā vilambena pratīteḥ, paramukhanirīkṣakatvāt/ syād api tasyā api prādhānyam, yadi vārivāhe niṣkaruṇatvādibodhakaṃ kiṃcid api syāt/ nāpi svapnasya, vārivāhanādena tannāśasyaiva pratipatteḥ/ astu vā svapnabhāvapraśamenāsūyayā ca sahāsya saṃkaraḥ/
idaṃ tu nodāhāryam--
"gāḍham āliṅgya sakalāṃ yāminīṃ saha tasthuṣīm/
nidrāṃ vihāya sa prātar āliliṅgātha cetanām//"
vibodhasya cetanāpadavācyatvāt/ yathā kaścit satyapratijño dvābhyāṃ nāyikābhyāṃ dvau kālāv upabhogārthaṃ dattvā yathocite kāla ekām upabhujya kālakantare pravṛtte tāṃ vihāyāparāṃ bhuṅkte, tathaivāyaṃ rātrau nidrāṃ prātaś cetanām iti samāsokter eveha prakāśanāt/
body.translated_text:
And the destruction of sleep is produced by sounds, touches, and the like that are powerful [enough to penetrate] the fulfillment of sleep and the interior of dreams — thus these very things are the <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) here. Rubbing the eyes, massaging the limbs, and so forth are the <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents).
Here is a brief illustration—
"Alas! Just as I am hearing the words of the fair-eyed one,
who had been granted to me today by the most beloved sleep in the last watch of the night,
at that very moment the thundercloud grew angry at me!"
Here, hearing the thunder is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The destruction of the delight of hearing the beloved's words is the <s>anubhāva</s>, to be inferred. Some authorities also recognize this [awakening] as produced by the destruction of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). In their view—
"Delusion is destroyed, memory is regained, by Your grace, O <s>Acyuta</s>;
I stand firm, free of doubt — I shall carry out Your command."
— this verse from the <s>Gītā</s> should be cited as illustration. But one should not suspect that the sentence meaning here is merely envy directed at the thundercloud. For when awakening is cognized, and when its inappropriateness in that context is understood, the envy toward the thundercloud — as the cause of inappropriate awakening — is cognized only with delay, since it is a secondary object of attention. That envy too might have prominence, only if there were some indication of mercilessness or the like in the thundercloud. Nor [is the primary meaning] about the dream, since from the sound of the thundercloud, only the destruction of the dream is apprehended. Or alternatively, let there be a mixture (<s>saṃkara</s>) of this [awakening] with the cessation of the dream-state (<s>svapnabhāva</s>) and with envy.
But this should not be cited as illustration—
"Having tightly embraced Sleep, who had stood with him the entire night,
he left her in the morning and then embraced Consciousness."
— because awakening (<s>vibodha</s>) is denoted by the word 'consciousness' (<s>cetanā</s>). Just as someone bound by a truthful promise, having allotted two periods to two heroines for enjoyment, enjoys one at the appointed time and, when the interval of the other period arrives, leaves that one and enjoys the other — in the same way, he [embraces] sleep at night and consciousness in the morning — because only the figure of <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression) is displayed here.

body.text: parakṛtāvajñādinānāparādhajanyo maunavākpāruṣyādikāraṇībhūtaś cittavṛttiviśeṣo 'marṣaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Amarṣa</s> (indignation) is a particular state of mind (<s>cittavṛtti</s>) born from various offenses such as contempt inflicted by others, which becomes the cause of silence, harsh speech, and the like.

body.text:
prāgvat
kāraṇānāṃ kāryāṇāṃ ca krameṇa vibhāvānubhāvatvam/
udāharaṇam--
"vakṣojāgraṃ pāṇināmṛṣya dūre yātasya drāgānanābjaṃ priyasya/
śoṇāgrābhyāṃ bhāminī locanābhyāṃ joṣaṃ joṣam joṣam evāvatasthe//"
iha tv ākasmikastanāgrasparśo vibhāvaḥ/ nayanāruṇyanirnimeṣanirīkṣaṇe anubhāvau/
nanu krodhāmarṣayoḥ sthāyisaṃcāriṇor bhāvayoḥ kiṃ bhedakam iti cet, viṣayatāvailakṣaṇyam eveti gṛhāṇa/ tatra tu gamakaṃ jhaṭiti paravināśādau pravṛttir vacanavaimukhyādikaṃ ceti kāryavailakṣaṇyam/
body.translated_text:
As before, the causes and effects are sequentially the <s>vibhāvas</s> and <s>anubhāvas</s>.
Illustration—
"Having touched the tip of her breast with his hand, of the beloved who has gone far away,
the fair-faced one silently, silently, just silently stood still, with her two reddened eyes."
Here the unexpected touching of the breast-tip is the <s>vibhāva</s>; the reddening of the eyes and the unwinking gaze are the two <s>anubhāvas</s>.
If one asks: what distinguishes <s>krodha</s> (anger) and <s>amarṣa</s> (indignation), which are respectively a permanent emotion (<s>sthāyī</s>) and a transitory one (<s>saṃcārī</s>)? — understand that it is precisely the difference of their objects. The indicator there is the difference of effects: in the former, there is immediate engagement in the destruction of the other, avoidance of speech, and so forth.

body.text: vrīḍādibhir nimittair harṣādyanubhāvānāṃ gopanāya janito bhāvaviśeṣo 'vahittham//
body.translated_text: <s>Avahittha</s> (dissimulation) is a particular emotional state generated for the purpose of concealing <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents) such as joy, by causes such as modesty and the like.

body.text:
taduktam--
"anubhāvapidhānārthe 'vahitthaṃ bhāva ucyate/
tadvibhāvyaṃ bhayavrīḍādhārṣṭyakauṭilyagauravaiḥ//"
yathā--
"prasaṅge gopānāṃ guruṣu mahimānaṃ yadupater
upākarṇya svidyatpulakitakapolā kulavadhūḥ/
viṣajvālājālaṃ jhagiti vamataḥ pannagapateḥ
phaṇāyāṃ sāścaryaṃ kathayatitarāṃ tāṇḍavavidhim//
body.translated_text:
As has been said—
"<s>Avahittha</s> is called a <s>bhāva</s> [generated] for the purpose of concealing <s>anubhāvas</s>;
it is to be recognized through fear, modesty, boldness, crookedness, and dignity."
As illustrated—
"In the course of [a conversation among] cowherds, when the elder women overhear the greatness of the Lord of the <s>Yadus</s>,
a young bride of the family, with cheeks perspiring and bristling with horripilation,
with great wonder narrates at length the manner of [His] <s>tāṇḍava</s> dance
upon the hood of the serpent-king who suddenly vomits a mass of fiery poison!"

body.text:
atra
vrīḍā vibhāvaḥ/ tādṛśakāliyakathāprasaṅgo 'nubhāvaḥ/ evaṃ bhayādiprayojyam apy udāhāryam/
body.translated_text: Here modesty (<s>vrīḍā</s>) is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The occasion of narrating the story of <s>Kāliya</s> in such a context is the <s>anubhāva</s>. Similarly, [dissimulation] prompted by fear and the like should also be illustrated.

body.text: adhikṣepāpamānādiprabhavā kim asya karomītyādyākārā cittavṛttir ugratā//
body.translated_text: <s>Ugratā</s> (fierceness) is a state of mind (<s>cittavṛtti</s>) arising from reproach, insult, and the like, of the form 'What shall I do to him!' and similar [impulses].

body.text:
yadāhuḥ--
"nṛpāparādho 'saddoṣakīrtanaṃ coradhāraṇam/
vibhāvāḥ syur atho bandho vadhas tāḍanabhanabhartsane//
body.translated_text:
As they have said—
"Offenses of the king, proclamation of false faults, and harboring thieves —
these are the <s>vibhāvas</s>; then imprisonment, killing, beating, and threatening

body.text:
ete yatrānubhāvās tadaugryaṃ nirdayatātmakam//" iti/
yathā--
"avāpya bhaṅgaṃ khalu saṃgarāṅgaṇe nitāntam aṅgādhipater amaṅgalam/
paraprabhāvaṃ mama gāṇḍivaṃ dhanur vinindatas te hṛdayaṃ na kampate//"
eṣā karṇena parābhūtaṃ gāṇḍivaṃ nindantaṃ yudhiṣṭhiraṃ prati dhanaṃjayasyoktiḥ/ yudhiṣṭhirakartṛkā gāṇḍivanindātra vibhāvaḥ/ vadhecchānubhāvaḥ/ na cāmarṣogratayor nāsti bheda iti vācyam/ prāg udāhṛte 'marṣadhvanāv ugratāyā apratīteḥ/ nāpy asau krodhaḥ/ tasya sthāyitvenāsyāḥ saṃcāriṇītvenaiva bhedāt/
body.translated_text:
— where these are the <s>anubhāvas</s>, that is <s>ugratā</s> (fierceness), whose nature is mercilessness."
As illustrated—
"Having suffered defeat in the battle-arena — truly most inauspicious — at the hands of the king of <s>Aṅga</s>,
your heart does not tremble as you revile my bow <s>Gāṇḍīva</s> [by calling it] dependent on another's power!"
This is the speech of <s>Dhanañjaya</s> (<s>Arjuna</s>) to <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, who was reviling <s>Gāṇḍīva</s> after being defeated by <s>Karṇa</s>. <s>Yudhiṣṭhira's</s> reviling of <s>Gāṇḍīva</s> is the <s>vibhāva</s> here; the desire to kill is the <s>anubhāva</s>. And one should not say there is no difference between <s>amarṣa</s> (indignation) and <s>ugratā</s> (fierceness), since in the previously cited illustration of <s>amarṣadhvani</s>, <s>ugratā</s> was not perceived. Nor is this <s>krodha</s> (anger), since <s>krodha</s> being a permanent emotion (<s>sthāyī</s>) and this being a transitory state (<s>saṃcāriṇī</s>) establishes their difference.

body.text: vipralambhamahāpattiparamānandādijanmā 'nyasminn anyāvabhāsa unmādaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Unmāda</s> (madness) is born from separation in love (<s>vipralambha</s>), great calamity, supreme bliss, and the like, and consists in the appearance of one thing as another.

body.text:
śuktirajatādijñānavyāvṛttaye janmāntam/
udāharaṇam--
"akaruṇahṛdaya priyatama muñcāmi tvām itaḥ paraṃ nāham/
ity ālapati karāmbujam ādāyālījanasya vikalā sā//"
eṣā
pravāsagataṃ svanāyikāvṛttāntaṃ pṛcchantaṃ nāyakaṃ prati kasyāścit saṃdeśahāriṇyā uktiḥ/ priyaviraho 'tra vibhāvaḥ/ asaṃbaddhoktir anubhāvaḥ/ unmādasya vyādhāv antarbhāve saṃbhavaty api pṛthag upādānaṃ vyādhyantarāpekṣayā vaicitryaviśeṣasphoraṇāya/
body.translated_text:
The qualification 'born from [something other than birth]' is to exclude cognitions like shell-silver [which is a perceptual error, not an emotional state].
Illustration—
"O hard-hearted beloved, I shall never leave you henceforth!
— so she prattles, distraught, taking the lotus-hand of one of her companions."
This is the speech of a certain female messenger to the hero who, having gone abroad, inquires about the state of his own heroine. Separation from the beloved is the <s>vibhāva</s> here; incoherent speech is the <s>anubhāva</s>. Even though <s>unmāda</s> (madness) could be subsumed under disease (<s>vyādhi</s>), it is enumerated separately to highlight its distinctive variety compared to other diseases.

body.text: rogādijanyā mūrchārūpā maraṇaprāgavasthā maraṇam//
body.translated_text: <s>Maraṇa</s> (death) is a state preceding death, having the nature of a swoon, produced by disease and the like.

body.text:
na cātra prāṇaviyogātmakaṃ mukhyaṃ maraṇam ucitaṃ grahītum/ cittavṛttyātmakeṣu bhāveṣu tasyāprasakteḥ/ bhāveṣu ca sarveṣu kāryasahavartitayā śarīraprāṇasaṃyogasya hetutvāt/
udāharaṇam--
"dayitasya guṇānanusmarantī śayane saṃprati yā vilokitāsīt/
adhunā khalu hanta sā kṛśāṅgī giram aṅgīkurute na bhāṣitāpi//"
priyaviraho 'tra vibhāva/ vacanavirāmo 'nubhāvaḥ/ hantapadasyātrātyantam upakārakatvād vākyavyaṅgyo 'py ayaṃ bhāvaḥ padavyaṅgyatām āvahati/ etena bhāvasya padavyaṅgyatāyāṃ nātyantaṃ vaicitryam iti parāstam/
dayitasya guṇān anusmarantīty anena vyajyamānaṃ "caramāvasthāyām api tasyā dayitaguṇavismaraṇaṃ nābhūd" iti vastu, vipralambhasya śokasya vā caramam abhivyaktasya poṣakam/ ayaṃ ca bhāvaḥ svavyañjakavākyottaravartinā vākyāntareṇa saṃdarbhaghaṭakena nāyikādeḥ pratyujjīvanavarṇane vipralambhasya, anyathā tu karuṇasya poṣaka iti vivekaḥ/ kavayaḥ punar amuṃ prādhānyena na varṇayanti, amaṅgalaprāyatvāt/
body.translated_text:
And here, death in its primary sense as the separation of the vital breath should not be understood, since it is inapplicable among the <s>bhāvas</s> whose nature is states of mind (<s>cittavṛtti</s>). And because in all <s>bhāvas</s>, the conjunction of body and vital breath is the cause [that enables them], as it accompanies the effect.
Illustration—
"She who was just seen on the bed, remembering the virtues of her beloved —
now, alas, that slender-limbed one does not accept speech, though spoken to!"
Separation from the beloved is the <s>vibhāva</s> here; cessation of speech is the <s>anubhāva</s>. Because the word 'hanta' (alas!) is extremely helpful here, this <s>bhāva</s>, though suggested by the sentence, also takes on the character of being suggested by a [single] word. By this, the [objection] that there is no great variety in a <s>bhāva</s> being word-suggested is set aside.
The phrase 'remembering the virtues of her beloved' suggests the real content (<s>vastu</s>) that 'even in her final state, she did not forget her beloved's virtues' — which nourishes the <s>vipralambha</s> (love-in-separation) or the <s>śoka</s> (grief) that is the ultimate suggested meaning. And this <s>bhāva</s>, by a subsequent sentence that forms part of the narrative context following the sentence that suggests it, nourishes <s>vipralambha</s> when the heroine's revival is described, and <s>karuṇa</s> (compassion) otherwise — this is the distinction. Poets, however, do not primarily depict this [bhāva], since it is mostly inauspicious.

body.text: saṃdehādyanantaraṃ jāyamāna ūho vitarkaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Vitarka</s> (conjecture) is a deliberation (<s>ūha</s>) that arises after doubt and the like.

body.text:
sa ca niścayānukūlaḥ/
"yadi sā mithilendranandinī nitarām eva na vidyate bhuvi/
body.translated_text:
And it is favorable to a conclusion.
"If that daughter of the lord of <s>Mithilā</s> truly does not exist on the earth at all,

body.text:
atha me katham asti jīvitaṃ na vinālambanam āśritasthitiḥ//"
svātmani bhagavato rāmasyaiṣoktiḥ/ bhuvi sītāsti na veti saṃdeho 'tra vibhāvaḥ/ bhrūkṣepaśiroṅgulinartanam ākṣiptam anubhāvaḥ/ na cāsau cinteti śakyaṃ vaditum, cintāyā niyamena niścayaṃ pratyaprayojakatvāt/ kiṃ bhaviṣyati kathaṃ bhaviṣyatīty ādy ākārāyāś cintāyāḥ, idam itthaṃ bhavitum arhati prāyaśa ityākārasya vitarkasya viṣayavailakṣaṇyopalambhāc ca/ na vinetyādinokto 'rthāntaranyāso 'py asminn evānukūlaḥ/
body.translated_text:
then how does my life persist? Existence without a support cannot be maintained!"
This is the speech of Lord <s>Rāma</s> to himself. The doubt 'Does <s>Sītā</s> exist on earth or not?' is the <s>vibhāva</s> here. The movement of eyebrows, head, and finger-dancing is the implied <s>anubhāva</s>. And one cannot call this <s>cintā</s> (anxiety), because <s>cintā</s> by its nature does not necessarily lead to a conclusion. And because we observe a difference of objects between <s>cintā</s>, whose forms are 'What will happen? How will it happen?' and <s>vitarka</s>, whose form is 'This must probably be thus.' The argument from negative concomitance ('not without') stated [in the verse] is also favorable to this [vitarka].

body.text: iṣṭāsiddhirājagurvādyaparādhādijanyo 'nutāpo viṣādaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Viṣāda</s> (dejection) is remorse born from failure to attain what is desired, offenses against the king or guru, and the like.

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"bhāskarasūnāv astaṃ yāte jāte ca pāṇḍavotkarṣe/
duryodhanasya jīvita katham iva nādyāpi niryāsi//"
atra svāpakarṣaparotkarṣayor darśanaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ jīvitaniryāṇāśaṃsā, tadākṣiptaṃ vadananamanādi cānubhāvaḥ/ asminn eva ca viṣādadhvanau duryodhanasyety arthāntarasaṃkramitavācyadhvanir anugrāhakaḥ/ na cātra trāsabhāvadhvanitvaṃ śakyam, paravīrasya duryodhanasya trāsaleśasyāpyayogāt/ nāpi cintādhvanitvam, yuddhvā mariṣyāmīti tasya vyavasāyāt/ nāpi dainyadhvanitvam, sakalasainyakṣaye 'pi vipadas tenāgaṇanāt/ na vā vīrarasadhvanitvam, maraṇasya śaraṇīkaraṇe parāpakarṣajīvitasyotsāhasyābhāvāt/
idaṃ punar atra nodāhāryam--
"ayi pavanarayāṇāṃ nirdayānāṃ hayānāṃ
ślathaya gatim ahaṃ no saṃgaraṃ draṣṭum īhe/
śrutivivaram amī me dārayanti prakupyad
bhujaganibhabhujānāṃ bāhujānāṃ ninādāḥ//
body.translated_text:
Illustration—
"When the son of the Sun (<s>Karṇa</s>) has set, and the ascendancy of the <s>Pāṇḍavas</s> has arisen,
O life of <s>Duryodhana</s>, how is it that you have not yet departed!"
Here, the sight of one's own decline and the other's ascendancy is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The wish for the departure of life, and the implied bowing of the face and the like, are the <s>anubhāvas</s>. And in this very <s>viṣādadhvani</s> (suggestion of dejection), the expression 'of <s>Duryodhana</s>' serves as a supporting <s>arthāntarasaṃkramitavācyadhvani</s> (suggestion through transference of expressed meaning to another meaning). And one cannot hold that this is the suggestion of the <s>bhāva</s> of fear (<s>trāsa</s>), because even a trace of fear is impossible in the hero-warrior <s>Duryodhana</s>. Nor is it the suggestion of <s>cintā</s> (anxiety), because of his resolve 'I shall fight and die.' Nor is it the suggestion of <s>dainya</s> (wretchedness), because he disregarded calamity even when his entire army was destroyed. Nor is it the suggestion of <s>vīrarasa</s> (heroic sentiment), because when death is the refuge, there is no <s>utsāha</s> (enthusiasm) for a life [marked by] the other's degradation.
But this should not be cited as illustration here—
"O charioteer, slacken the pace of these merciless horses of <s>Pavana's</s> son;
I do not wish to witness the battle.
These roars of those whose arms are like angry serpents
are splitting my ears!"

body.text:
atra trāsasyaiva pratīyamānatvena
viṣādasyāpratīteḥ/ leśatayā pratitau vā trāsa evānuguṇyaucityena dhvanivyapadeśāyogyatvāt/
body.translated_text: Here, since only <s>trāsa</s> (fear/fright) is apprehended, <s>viṣāda</s> (despondency) is not perceived. Or even if perceived to a slight degree, <s>trāsa</s> alone, by virtue of its suitability and propriety, is unfit for the designation of <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion).

body.text: adhunaivāsya lābho mamāstv itīcchā autsukyam//
body.translated_text: The desire "may I obtain this right now" is <s>autsukyam</s> (eagerness).

body.text:
iṣṭavirahādir atra vibhāvaḥ/ tvarācintādayo 'nubhāvāḥ/
yadāhuḥ--
"saṃjātam iṣṭavirahād uddīptaṃ priyasaṃsmṛteḥ/
nidrayā tandrayā gātragauraveṇa ca cintayā//
body.translated_text:
Separation from a desired object and the like is the <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant) here. Haste, anxiety, and similar states are the <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents).
As they say—
"Arising from separation from the desired, kindled by the recollection of the beloved, through sleepiness, lethargy, heaviness of limbs, and anxiety,

body.text:
anubhāvitam ākhyātam autsukyaṃ bhāvakovidaiḥ//" iti/
udāharaṇam--
"nipatadbāṣpasaṃrodham uktacāñcalyatārakam/
kadā nayananīlābjam ālokeya mṛgīdṛśaḥ//"
body.translated_text:
manifested thus, <s>autsukyam</s> (eagerness) has been described by those learned in emotions." Thus.
An illustration—
"When shall I see the blue lotus-eye of the doe-eyed one, with falling tears restrained and with pupils declared to be restless?"

body.text: anarthātiśayajanitā cittasya saṃbhramākhyā vṛttir āvegaḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Āvega</s> (agitation) is a mental state called <s>saṃbhrama</s> (fluster), born from an excess of calamity.

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"līlayā vihitasindhubandhana so 'yam eti raghuvaṃśanandanaḥ/
darpadurvilasito daśānanaḥ kutra yāmi nikaṭe kulakṣayaḥ//
body.translated_text:
An illustration—
"He who playfully built the bridge across the ocean, that joy of the <s>Raghu</s> dynasty, is coming! Where shall I go, I whose arrogance has been ill-displayed? The destruction of my race is near!"

body.text:
eṣā svātmani mandodaryā uktiḥ/ raghunandanāgamanam atra vibhāvaḥ/
kutra yāmīty etad vyaṅgyaḥ sthairyābhāvo 'nubhāvaḥ/ na cātra cintā prādhānyena vyajyata iti śakyate vaktum, kutra yāmīti sphuṭaṃ pratītena sthairyābhāvenodvegasyeva cintāyā apratyāyanāt/ paraṃ tv āvegacarvaṇāyāṃ tatparipoṣakatayā guṇatvena cintāpi viṣayībhavati/
body.translated_text: This is the speech of <s>Mandodarī</s> to herself. The arrival of the scion of <s>Raghu</s> is the <s>vibhāva</s> here. "Where shall I go?"—this suggested absence of steadiness is the <s>anubhāva</s>. Nor can it be said that anxiety is predominantly suggested here, because the absence of steadiness clearly perceived through "Where shall I go?" fails to convey anxiety just as it fails to convey agitation. However, in the relishing of <s>āvega</s>, anxiety too becomes an object in a subordinate capacity as something that nourishes it.

body.text: cintotkaṇṭhābhayaviraheṣṭāniṣṭadarśanaśravaṇādijanyāvaśyakartavyārthapratisaṃdhānavikalā cittavṛttir jaḍatā//
body.translated_text: <s>Jaḍatā</s> (stupor) is the mental state characterized by the inability to deliberate on necessary courses of action, born from anxiety, longing, fear, separation, seeing or hearing of desired or undesired things, and so on.

body.text:
iyaṃ ca mohāt pūrvataḥ parataś ca jāyate/
yad āha--
"kāryāviveko jaḍatā pasyataḥ śṛṇvato 'pi vā/
tadvibhāvāḥ priyāniṣṭadarśanaśravaṇe rujā//
body.translated_text:
And this arises both before and after <s>moha</s> (delusion).
As stated—
"<s>Jaḍatā</s> is the inability to discriminate what is to be done, even while seeing or hearing. Its <s>vibhāvas</s> are the seeing or hearing of a beloved's misfortune, and suffering.

body.text:
anubhāvās tv amī tūṣṇīṃ bhāvavismaraṇādayaḥ/
sā pūrvaṃ parato vā syān mohād iti vidāṃ matam//"
udāharaṇam--
"yad avadhi dayito vilocanābhyāṃ sahacari daivavaśena dūrato 'bhūt/
tad avadhi śithilīkṛto madīyair atha karaṇaiḥ praṇayo nijakriyāsu//"
priyaviraho 'tra vibhāvaḥ/ karaṇaiś cakṣuḥśravaṇādibhiḥ kriyāsu tattatpramitiṣu praṇayasya śithilīkaraṇam anubhāvaḥ/ mohe cakṣurādibhiś cākṣuṣāder ajananam, iha
tu prakāraviśeṣavaiśiṣṭyena bāhulyenājananam iti tasmād asya viśeṣaḥ/ ata evodāharaṇe śithilīkṛta ity uktam, na tu tyakta iti/
body.translated_text:
Its <s>anubhāvas</s> are silence, forgetting of emotions, and the like. It may occur before or after <s>moha</s>—such is the view of the learned."
An illustration—
"O companion, from the time when my beloved, by the force of fate, became distant from my eyes, from that time onward, the affection of my faculties for their own functions has been slackened."
The separation from the beloved is the <s>vibhāva</s> here. The slackening of engagement by the faculties—the eyes, ears, and others—in their respective activities of perception is the <s>anubhāva</s>. In <s>moha</s>, the faculties such as the eye fail to produce their respective cognitions altogether, but here the distinction is that they fail to produce them in a particular manner and in abundance. For this very reason, the illustration uses the word "slackened" and not "abandoned."

body.text: atitṛptigarbhavyādhiśramādijanyā cetasaḥ kriyānunmukhatālasyam//
body.translated_text: <s>Ālasyam</s> (indolence) is the mind's disinclination toward action, born from excessive satiation, pregnancy, illness, fatigue, and the like.

body.text:
atra ca nāsāmarthyam/ nāpi kāryākāryavivekaśūnyatvam/ tena kāryākaraṇarūpasyānubhāvasya tulyatve 'pi glāner jaḍatāyāś cāsya bhedaḥ/
udāharaṇam--
"nikhilāṃ
rajanīṃ priyeṇa dūrād upayātena vibodhitā kathābhiḥ/
adhikaṃ na hi pārayāmi vaktuṃ sakhi mā jalpa tavāyasī rasajñā//"
eṣā hi priyāgamanadvitīyadivase muhurniśāvṛttāntaṃ pṛcchantīṃ sakhīṃ prati rajanijāgaraṇajanitālasyāyāḥ kasyāścid uktiḥ/ atra rajanijāgaraṇaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ adhikasaṃbhāṣaṇābhāvo 'nubhāvaḥ/ jaḍatāyāṃ mohāt pūrvavartitvam uttaravartitvaṃ vā niyatam, na tv atrety aparo viśeṣaḥ/ gopanīyaviṣayatvād yadi kathābhir ity avivakṣitavācyaṃ tadā śramo 'stu paripoṣakaḥ/ śramajanye hy ālasye śramasya poṣakatāyā avāryatvāt/ atitṛptyādijanite tv ālasye śramād viviktaviṣayatvaṃ bodhyam/
body.translated_text:
Here there is neither incapacity nor the absence of discrimination between what should and should not be done. Therefore, although the <s>anubhāva</s> of not performing actions is the same, <s>glāni</s> (languor), <s>jaḍatā</s> (stupor), and this (<s>ālasya</s>) are distinct.
An illustration—
"Having been kept awake the entire night by my beloved who came from afar, with conversations—I cannot speak more, O friend, do not chatter, are you made of iron, you connoisseur of sentiments?"
This is the utterance of a certain woman to her friend who keeps asking about the events of the night, on the second day after the beloved's arrival, she being affected by indolence born from staying awake all night. Here the night-long wakefulness is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The inability to converse further is the <s>anubhāva</s>. In <s>jaḍatā</s>, occurring either before or after <s>moha</s> is obligatory, but not here—this is another distinction. If the expression "with conversations" is intended as a case where the subject matter is to be concealed, then fatigue may be the nourishing factor. For in indolence born from fatigue, the nourishing quality of fatigue cannot be denied. But in indolence born from excessive satiation and the like, it should be understood that the domain is distinct from that of fatigue.

body.text: parotkarṣadarśanādijanyaḥ paranindādikāraṇībhūtaś cittavṛttiviśeṣo 'sūyā//
body.translated_text: <s>Asūyā</s> (envy) is a particular mental state born from seeing the excellence of others and the like, which becomes the cause of disparaging others.

body.text:
imām evāsahanādiśabdair vyavaharanti/
yathā--
"kutra śaivaṃ dhanur idaṃ kva cāyaṃ prākṛtaḥ śiśuḥ/
bhaṅgas tu sarvasaṃhartrā kālenaiva vinirmitaḥ//"
eṣā bhagnaharakārmukasya bhagavato rāmasya parākramam asahamānānāṃ tatratyānāṃ rājñām uktiḥ/ atra ca śrīmaddāśarathibalasya sarvotkṛṣṭatāyā darśanaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ prākṛtaśiśupadagamyā nindā anubhāvaḥ/
"tṛṣṇālolavilocane kalayati prācīṃ cakoravraje
maunaṃ muñcati kiṃ ca kairavakule kāme dhanur dhunvati/
māne mānavatījanasya sapadi prasthātukāme 'dhūnā
dhātaḥ kiṃ nu vidhau vidhātum ucito dhārādharāḍambaraḥ//"
atrāpi yady api tadīyocchṛṅkhalatādidarśanajanyā anucitakāritvarūpanindāprakāśānubhāvitā
kavigatā vidhātrālambanāsūyā vyajyata iti śakyate vaktum, tathāpi kāryakāraṇayos tulyatvād abhivyaktenāmarṣeṇa śabalitaivāsau
na viviktatayā pratiyate/ nahi vidhātur aparādha iva bhagavato rāmasyāparādho 'sti yena kaver iva vīrāṇām apy amarṣo 'bhivyajyeta/ svabhāvo hi mahonnatakriyāniṣpādanaṃ vīrāṇām/ atrāprastutacandravṛttāntena prastutarājakumārādivṛttāntasya dhvananān nāsty asūyādhvanitvam iti tu na vācyam/ ekadhvaner dhvanyantarāvirodhitvāt/ anyathā mahāvākyadhvaner avāntaravākyadhvanibhiḥ, teṣāṃ ca padadhvanibhiḥ saha sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ kutrāpi na syāt/
body.translated_text:
This is also expressed by words such as <s>asahana</s> (intolerance) and others.
For example—
"Where is this bow of <s>Śiva</s>, and where is this common child? The breaking was surely brought about by <s>Kāla</s> (Time), the destroyer of all!"
This is the speech of the kings who could not tolerate the prowess of Lord <s>Rāma</s> who had broken the bow of <s>Hara</s>. Here, the sight of the surpassing strength of the glorious son of <s>Daśaratha</s> is the <s>vibhāva</s>. The disparagement conveyed by the words "common child" is the <s>anubhāva</s>.
"When the <s>cakora</s> bird-flock turns its eyes thirsty with longing toward the east, when the water-lily cluster abandons its silence, when <s>Kāma</s> (Love) bends his bow, when the pride of proud women suddenly prepares to depart—O Creator, is this display of rain-clouds now fitting to ordain?"
Here too, although it could be said that <s>asūyā</s> (envy) toward the Creator as <s>ālambana</s>, belonging to the poet and manifested through the <s>anubhāva</s> of revealing blame in the form of causing inappropriate actions—born from witnessing His unruliness and the like—is suggested, nevertheless, due to the equality of the effect and cause, that envy is perceived as tinged with <s>amarṣa</s> (indignation) rather than in its pure form. For there is no offense of Lord <s>Rāma</s> as there is of the Creator, such that indignation would be suggested in the warriors as it is in the poet. For the nature of warriors is the accomplishment of great and lofty deeds. And it should not be said that because the present narrative about the moon suggests by implication the narrative about the prince and others, there is no suggestion of envy—for one type of <s>dhvani</s> is not incompatible with another. Otherwise, the co-occurrence of <s>dhvani</s> of a great sentence with <s>dhvanis</s> of subordinate sentences, and of those with <s>dhvanis</s> of individual words, would never be possible anywhere.

body.text: viyogaśokabhayajugupsādīnām atiśayād grahāveśādeś cotpanno vyādhiviśeṣo 'pasmāraḥ//
body.translated_text: <s>Apasmāra</s> (epileptic seizure) is a particular illness arising from the excess of separation, grief, fear, disgust, and the like, as well as from spirit-possession and similar causes.

body.text:
vyādhitvenāsya kathane 'pi viśeṣākāreṇa punaḥ kathanaṃ bībhatsabhayānakayor asyaiva vyādher aṅgatvaṃ nānyasyeti sphoraṇāya/ vipralambhe tu vyādhyantarasyāpi ca/ udāharaṇam--
"harim āgatam ākarṇya mathurām antakāntakam/
kampamānaḥ śvasan kaṃso nipapāta mahītale//"
atra bhayaṃ vibhāvaḥ/ kampaniḥśvāsapatanādayo 'nubhāvāḥ/
body.translated_text:
Even though this has been described as a disease, the reason for describing it again in a specific manner is to make clear that in <s>bībhatsa</s> (disgust) and <s>bhayānaka</s> (terror), only this particular disease serves as a component, not any other. But in <s>vipralambha</s> (love-in-separation), other diseases also serve as components.
An illustration—
"Hearing that <s>Hari</s>, the destroyer of Death's destroyer, had arrived at <s>Mathurā</s>, <s>Kaṃsa</s>, trembling and gasping, fell to the ground."
Here fear is the <s>vibhāva</s>. Trembling, heavy breathing, and falling are the <s>anubhāvas</s>.

body.text: amarṣādijanyavākpāruṣyādikāraṇībhūtā cittavṛttiś capalatā//
body.translated_text: <s>Capalatā</s> (rashness) is a mental state that becomes the cause of harshness of speech and the like, born from <s>amarṣa</s> (indignation) and similar emotions.

body.text:
yad āhu--
"amarṣaprātikūlyerṣyārāgadveṣāś ca matsaraḥ/
iti yatra vibhāvāḥ syur anubhāvas tu bhartsanam//
body.translated_text:
As they say—
"Where <s>amarṣa</s> (indignation), hostility, <s>īrṣyā</s> (jealousy), passion, hatred, and <s>matsara</s> (malice) are the <s>vibhāvas</s>, and the <s>anubhāvas</s> are threatening,

body.text:
vākpāruṣyaṃ prahāraś ca tāḍanaṃ vadhabandhane/
taccāpalam
anālocya kāryakāritvam iṣyate//" iti/
udāharaṇam--
"ahitavrata pāpātman maivaṃ me darśayānanam/
ātmānaṃ hantum icchāmi yena tvam asi bhāvitaḥ//"
eṣā bhagavadanuraktivighaṭanopāyam apaśyataḥ prahlādaṃ prati hiraṇyakaśipor uktiḥ/ bhagavaddveṣotthāpitaḥ putradveṣo 'tra vibhāvaḥ/ ātmavadhecchā paruṣavacanaṃ cānubhāvaḥ/ na cāmarṣa evātra vyajyata iti vācyam/
sadaiva bhagavadanurāgiṇi prahlāde hiraṇyakaśipor amarṣasya cirakālasaṃbhṛtatvenātmavadhecchāyā idaṃprathamatānupapatteḥ/
idaṃprathamakāryasya cedaṃprathamakāraṇaprayojyatayā prācīnacittavṛttivilakṣaṇāyā eva capalatākhyacittavṛtteḥ siddheḥ/ na cāmarṣaprakarṣa evātmavadhecchādikāraṇam abhivyajyatām iti vācyam/ prakarṣasyāpi svābhāvikavilakṣaṇalakṣaṇatāyā āvaśyakatayā tasyaiva capalatāpadārthatvāt/
nīcapuruṣeṣv

children.text: ākrośanādhikṣepavyādhitāḍanadāridryeṣṭavirahaparasaṃpaddarśanādibhiḥ, uttameṣu tv avajñādibhir janitā viṣayadveṣākhyā rodanadīrghaśvāsadīnamukhatādikāriṇī cittavṛttir nirvedaḥ/
children.translated_text: <s>Nirveda</s> (despondency) is a mental state called aversion toward the object, produced by abuse, reproach, illness, beating, poverty, separation from the desired, seeing the prosperity of others, and the like—but in noble persons, by disrespect and similar causes—which gives rise to weeping, deep sighing, a dejected face, and so on.

body.translated_text:
harshness of speech, striking, beating, killing, and binding—that <s>cāpala</s> (rashness) is understood as acting without deliberation on what should be done." Thus.
An illustration—
"O you of evil vows, O wicked soul, do not show me your face thus! I wish to kill myself, by whom you have been conceived."
This is the speech of <s>Hiraṇyakaśipu</s> to <s>Prahlāda</s>, who sees no means of disrupting his devotion to the Lord. Hatred of his son, aroused by hatred of the Lord, is the <s>vibhāva</s> here. The desire to kill himself and the harsh words are the <s>anubhāvas</s>. Nor should it be said that only <s>amarṣa</s> (indignation) is suggested here, because since <s>Prahlāda</s> has always been devoted to the Lord, <s>Hiraṇyakaśipu's</s> <s>amarṣa</s> has long been accumulated, and therefore the desire to kill himself cannot be something occurring for the first time.
Since the effect occurring for the first time must be produced by a cause occurring for the first time, a mental state called <s>capalatā</s>, which is distinct from the preceding mental state, is established. Nor should it be said that an excess of <s>amarṣa</s> itself is the cause that is being suggested for the desire to kill himself and the like, because that excess too, being characterized by a distinctive character different from the natural state, is precisely what constitutes the meaning of the term <s>capalatā</s>.
In persons of low character,

body.text:
udāharaṇam--
"yadi lakṣmaṇa sā mṛgekṣaṇā na madīkṣāsaraṇiṃ sameṣyati/
amunā jaḍajīvitena me jagatā vā viphalena kiṃ phalam//"
nityānityavastuvivekajanyatvābhāvān nāsau rasavyapadeśahetuḥ/
devādiviṣayā ratir yathā--
"bhavaddvāri
krudhyajjayavijayadaṇḍāhatidalat-
kirīṭās te kīṭā iva vidhimahendraprabhṛtayaḥ/
vitiṣṭhante yuṣman nayanaparipātotkalikayā
varākāḥ ke tatra kṣapitamura nākādhipatayaḥ//"
atrāpamānasahanabhagavaddvāraniṣevaṇabhagavatkaṭākṣapātābhilāṣādibhir brahmādigatā bhagavadālambanā ratir nābhivyajyate, api tu bhagavadaiśvaryam avāṅmanasagocara iti cet tathāpi tādṛśabhagavadaiśvaryavarṇanānubhāvitayā kavigatabhagavadālambanaratyā dhvanitvam akṣatam eva/
idaṃ vodāharaṇam--
"na dhanaṃ na ca rājyasaṃpadaṃ na hi vidyām idam ekam arthaye/
mayi dhehi manāg api prabho karuṇābhaṅgitaraṅgitāṃ dṛśam//"
atra dhanādyapekṣāśūnyasya bhagavaddṛgantapātābhilāṣo hi bhagavaty atyantānuraktiṃ vyanakti/ evaṃ saṃkṣepeṇa nirūpitā bhāvāḥ//
body.translated_text: An example: "O <s>Lakṣmaṇa</s>, if that doe-eyed one will not come into the path of my gaze, what fruit is there from this inert life of mine, or from this fruitless world?" Because this [<s>nirveda</s>, world-weariness] does not arise from the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things, it is not a ground for the designation of <s>rasa</s> [i.e., <s>śāntarasa</s>]. An example of <s>rati</s> (love) directed toward gods and the like: "At Your door, with their crowns shattered by the blows of the staff of the angry <s>Jaya</s> and <s>Vijaya</s>, like insects, <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Mahendra</s>, and the others stand, with the eager desire for a side-glance from Your eyes—O destroyer of <s>Mura</s>, who then are those wretched lords of heaven?" If one says that here, through the endurance of insult, the attendance at the Lord's door, and the desire for the Lord's side-glance, the <s>rati</s> directed toward the Lord as <s>ālambana</s> (substrate), belonging to <s>Brahmā</s> and the others, is not being manifested, but rather the Lord's majesty beyond the reach of speech and mind [is being manifested]—even so, the <s>dhvani</s> status remains intact through the poet's own <s>rati</s> toward the Lord as <s>ālambana</s>, which is realized through the description of such divine majesty. Or this may be the example: "Neither wealth, nor the prosperity of kingship, nor learning do I seek—this one thing alone I entreat: O Lord, cast upon me even a slight glance rippling with waves of compassion." Here, the desire for a mere side-glance of the Lord, on the part of one devoid of any expectation of wealth and the like, suggests the most intense devotion (<s>anurakti</s>) to the Lord. Thus the <s>bhāvas</s> (transitory emotions) have been briefly examined.

body.text:
atha katham asya saṃkhyāniyamaḥ/ mātsaryodvegadambherṣyāvivekanirṇayaklaibyakṣamākutukotkaṇṭhāvinayasaṃśayadhārṣṭyādīnām api tatra tatra lakṣyeṣu darśanāt iti cet, na/ ukteṣv evaiṣām antarbhāveṇa saṃkhyāntarānupapatteḥ/ asūyāto mātsaryasya, trāsād udvegasya, avahitthākhyād bhāvād dambhasya, amarṣād īrṣyāyāḥ, mater vivekanirṇayayoḥ, dainyāt klaibyasya, dhṛteḥ kṣamāyāḥ, autsukyāt kutukotkaṇṭhayoḥ, lajjāyā vinayasya, tarkāt saṃśayasya, cāpalād dhārṣṭyasya ca vastutaḥ sūkṣme bhede 'pi nāntarīyakatayā tadanatiriktasyaivādhyavasāyāt/ munivacanānupālanasya saṃbhava ucchṛṅkhalatāyā anaucityāt/ eṣu ca saṃcāribhāveṣu madhye kecana keṣāṃcana vibhāvā anubhāvāś ca
bhavanti/
tathā hi-- īrṣyāyā nirvedaṃ prati vibhāvatvam, asūyāṃ prati cānubhāvatvam/ cintāyā nidrāṃ prati vibhāvatvam, autsukyaṃ prati cānubhāvatetyādi svayam ūhyam/
atha rasābhāsaḥ-- tatra
body.translated_text: Now, how is the number [of <s>bhāvas</s>] fixed? If one objects that jealousy (<s>mātsarya</s>), perturbation (<s>udvega</s>), hypocrisy (<s>dambha</s>), envy (<s>īrṣyā</s>), discernment (<s>viveka</s>), determination (<s>nirṇaya</s>), impotence (<s>klaibya</s>), forbearance (<s>kṣamā</s>), curiosity (<s>kutuka</s>), longing (<s>utkaṇṭhā</s>), modesty (<s>vinaya</s>), doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>), audacity (<s>dhārṣṭya</s>), and others are also seen in various literary examples—[we reply:] No. Because these are subsumed within the ones already stated, and no additional number can be established. <s>Mātsarya</s> (jealousy) within <s>asūyā</s> (envy); <s>udvega</s> (perturbation) within <s>trāsa</s> (terror); <s>dambha</s> (hypocrisy) within the <s>bhāva</s> called <s>avahitthā</s> (dissimulation); <s>īrṣyā</s> (envy) within <s>amarṣa</s> (indignation); <s>viveka</s> (discernment) and <s>nirṇaya</s> (determination) within <s>mati</s> (cogitation); <s>klaibya</s> (impotence) within <s>dainya</s> (despondency); <s>kṣamā</s> (forbearance) within <s>dhṛti</s> (fortitude); <s>kutuka</s> (curiosity) and <s>utkaṇṭhā</s> (longing) within <s>autsukyā</s> (eagerness); <s>vinaya</s> (modesty) within <s>lajjā</s> (shame); <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) within <s>tarka</s> (conjecture); and <s>dhārṣṭya</s> (audacity) within <s>cāpala</s> (fickleness)—because even though there is a subtle difference in reality, due to necessary concomitance, what is not distinct from those is what is determined [as the bhāva]. The preservation of the sages' statements is possible [this way], since unrestrained [proliferation] would be improper. And among these transitory emotions (<s>saṃcāribhāvas</s>), some serve as <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) and <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents) of others. That is to say: <s>īrṣyā</s> (envy) is a <s>vibhāva</s> with respect to <s>nirveda</s> (world-weariness) and an <s>anubhāva</s> with respect to <s>asūyā</s> (envy); <s>cintā</s> (anxiety) is a <s>vibhāva</s> with respect to <s>nidrā</s> (sleep) and an <s>anubhāva</s> with respect to <s>autsukyā</s> (eagerness)—and so on, to be inferred by oneself. Now, <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of <s>rasa</s>)—regarding that:

body.text: anucitavibhāvālambanatvaṃ rasābhāsatvam//
body.translated_text: The nature of <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of <s>rasa</s>) is having an improper <s>vibhāva</s> as <s>ālambana</s> (substrate).

body.text:
vibhāvādāv anaucityaṃ punar lokānāṃ vyavahārato vijñeyam/ yatra teṣām ayuktam iti dhīr iti kecid āhuḥ/ tad apare na kṣamante/ munipatnyādiviṣayakaratyādeḥ saṃgrahe 'pi bahunāyakaviṣayāyā anubhayaniṣṭhāyāś ca rater asaṃgrahāt/ tatra vibhāvagatasyānaucityasyābhāvāt/ tasmād anaucityena ratyādir viśeṣaṇīyaḥ/ itthaṃ cānucitavibhāvālambanāyā bahunāyakaviṣayāyā anubhayaniṣṭhāyāś ca saṃgraha iti/ anaucityaṃ ca prāgvad eva/ tatra rasādyābhāsatvaṃ rasatvādinā na samānādhikaraṇam/ nirmalasyaiva rasāditvāt/ "hetvābhāsatvam iva hetutvena" ity eke/ "na hy anucitatvenātmahāniḥ, api tu sadoṣatvād ābhāsavyavahāraḥ/ aśvābhāsādivyavahāravat" ity apare/
udāharaṇam--
"śatenopāyānāṃ katham api gataḥ saudhaśikharaṃ
sudhāphenasvacche rahasi śayitāṃ puṣpaśayane/
vibodhya kṣāmāṅgīṃ cakitanayanāṃ smeravadanāṃ
saniḥśvāsaṃ śliṣyaty ahaha sukṛtī rājaramaṇīm//"
atrālambanam anucitapraṇayā rājaramaṇī/ rahorajanyādy uddīpanam/ sāhasena rājāntaḥpure gamanam, prāṇeṣūpekṣā, niḥśvāsāśleṣādayaś cānubhāvāḥ/ śaṅkādayaḥ saṃcāriṇaḥ/ niṣiddhālambanakatvāc cāsyā rateḥ, ābhāsatvaṃ rasasya/ na cātra cakitanayanām ity anena parapuruṣasparśatrāsābhivyaktyā rater anubhayaniṣṭhatety ābhāsatāhetur vācyaḥ/
asyāś ca cirāya tasminn āsaktāyā antaḥpure parapuruṣāgamanasyātyantam asaṃbhāvanayā ka eṣa māṃ bodhayatīty ādāv ucita eva trāsaḥ/ anantaraṃ ca paricayābhivyaktyā so 'yaṃ matpriyo madarthaṃ prāṇān api tṛṇīkṛtyāgata iti jñānād utpannaṃ harṣam abhivyañjayat smeravadanām iti viśeṣaṇaṃ ratiṃ tadīyām api vyanakti/ paraṃ tu prādhānyaṃ nāyakaniṣṭhāyā eva rateḥ, sakalavākyārthatvāt/
yathā vā--
"bhavanaṃ karuṇāvatī viśantī gamanājñālavalābhalālaseṣu/
taruṇeṣu vilocanābjamālām atha bālā pathi pātayāṃbabhūva//
body.translated_text: The impropriety in the <s>vibhāva</s> and the rest is to be understood from the conduct of the world. Some say it is where people have the cognition "this is improper." Others do not accept that. Because even though [that definition] would include <s>rati</s> (love) directed toward the wife of a sage and the like, it would fail to include <s>rati</s> directed toward multiple <s>nāyakas</s> (heroes), and <s>rati</s> that resides in neither [of the two parties]. Because in those cases, there is no impropriety in the <s>vibhāva</s>. Therefore, <s>rati</s> and the rest must be qualified by impropriety [in general]. Thus, <s>rati</s> with an improper <s>vibhāva</s> as <s>ālambana</s>, <s>rati</s> directed toward multiple <s>nāyakas</s>, and <s>rati</s> residing in neither party are all included. And impropriety is as previously [defined]. In this regard, the status of being a <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance) and the like is not co-predicated with being a <s>rasa</s> and the like. Because only what is pure is [truly] <s>rasa</s> and so forth. Some say: "Like the relation of a fallacious reason (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) to a valid reason (<s>hetu</s>)." Others say: "It is not that there is self-destruction through impropriety, but rather, due to being defective, the designation 'semblance' (<s>ābhāsa</s>) is applied—just as in the usage of 'semblance of a horse' (<s>aśvābhāsa</s>) and the like." An example: "Having reached the palace rooftop by a hundred stratagems, in secret, on a flower-bed white as the foam of nectar, waking the emaciated woman with startled eyes and a smiling face, with a sigh he embraces—ah!—the fortunate one, the king's consort." Here, the <s>ālambana</s> (substrate) is the king's consort toward whom love is improper. The <s>uddīpana</s> (excitant) is the seclusion, nighttime, and so forth. The <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents) are the daring entry into the king's inner chambers, the disregard for one's life, the sighing embrace, and the like. The <s>saṃcārins</s> (transitory emotions) are apprehension (<s>śaṅkā</s>) and others. Because this <s>rati</s> has a forbidden <s>ālambana</s>, the <s>rasa</s> is a semblance (<s>ābhāsa</s>). Nor should one say that here, by the expression "with startled eyes," the manifestation of fear from the touch of another man [shows that] the <s>rati</s> resides in neither party, and that this is the cause of its being a semblance. For this woman, who has been attached to him for a long time, considering the arrival of another man in the inner chambers to be utterly impossible, the initial fear of "who is this waking me?" is entirely appropriate. And then, the qualifier "with a smiling face," manifesting <s>harṣa</s> (joy) born from the recognition that "this is my beloved who has come disregarding even his life for my sake," also suggests her <s>rati</s> (love). But the predominance belongs to the <s>rati</s> residing in the <s>nāyaka</s> (hero), since it is the meaning of the entire sentence. Or for example: "The compassionate young girl, entering the house, cast the garland of her lotus eyes upon the path, at the young men who were eager with the slightest hope of a command to depart."

body.text:
atra kutaś cid āgacchantyāḥ pathi tadīyarūpayauvanagṛhītamānasair yuvabhir anugamyamānāyāḥ kasyāś cid bhavanapraveśasamaye nijasevāsārthakyavijñānāya gamanājñāpanarūpalābhalālaseṣu teṣu paramapariśramasmaraṇasaṃjātakaruṇāyā gamanājñādānanivedakasya vilocanāmbujamālāparikṣepasyānubhāvasya varṇanād abhivyajyamānā ratir bahuvacanena bahuviṣayā gamyata iti bhavaty ayam api rasābhāsaḥ/
yathā vā--
"bhujapañjare gṛhītā navapariṇītā vareṇa vadhūḥ/
tatkālajālapatitā bālakuraṅgīva vepate nitarām//"
atra rater navavadhvā manāg apy asparśād anubhayaniṣṭhatvenābhāsatvam/
yathā coktam--
"upanāyakasaṃsthāyāṃ munigurupatnīgatāyāṃ ca/
bahunāyakaviṣayāyāṃ ratau tathānubhayaniṣṭhāyām//" iti/
atra muniguruśabdayor upalakṣaṇaparatayā rājāder api
grahaṇam/
athātra kiṃ vyaṅgyam--
"vyānamrāś calitāś caiva sphāritāḥ paramākulāḥ/
pāṇḍuputreṣu pāñcālyāḥ patanti prathamā dṛśaḥ//"
atra vyānamratayā dharmātmatāprayojyaṃ yudhiṣṭhire sabhaktitvam, calitatayā sthūlākāratāprayojyaṃ bhīmasene satrāsatvam, sphāritatayā alaukikaśauryaśravaṇaprayojyam arjune saharṣatvam, paramākulatayā paramasaundaryaprayojyaṃ nakulasahadevayor autsukyaṃ ca vyañjayantībhir dṛgbhiḥ pāñcālyā bahuviṣayāyā rater abhivyañjanād rasābhāsa eveti navyāḥ/ prāñcas tv apariṇetṛbahunāyakaviṣayatve rater ābhāsatety āhuḥ/ tatra śṛṅgārarasa iva śṛṅgārābhāso 'pi dvividhaḥ/ saṃyogavipralambhabhedāt/ saṃyogābhāsas tv anupadam evodāhṛtaḥ/
vipralambhābhāso yathā--
"vyatyastaṃ lapati kṣaṇaṃ kṣaṇam atho maunaṃ samālambate
sarvasmin vidadhāti kiṃ ca viṣaye dṛṣṭi nirālambanām/
śvāsaṃ dīrgham urīkaroti na manāg aṅgeṣu dhatte dhṛtiṃ
vaidehīkamanīyatākavalito hā hanta laṅkeśvaraḥ//"
atra sītālambaneyaṃ laṅkeśagatā vipralambharatir anubhayaniṣṭhatayā jagadgurupatnīviṣayakatayā cābhāsatāṃ gatā, vyatyastaṃ lapatīty ādibhir uktibhir vyajyamānair unmādaśramamohacintāvyādhibhis tathaivābhāsatāṃ gataiḥ prādhānyena paripoṣyamāṇā dhvanivyapadeśahetuḥ/ evaṃ kalahaśīlakuputrādyālambanatayā vītarāgādiniṣṭhatayā ca varṇyamānaḥ śokaḥ, brahmavidyānadhikāricāṇḍālādigatatvena ca nirvedaḥ, kadaryakātarādigatatvena pitrādyālambanatvena vā krodhotsāhau, aindrajālikādyālambanatvena ca vismayaḥ, gurvādyālambanatayā ca hāsaḥ,
mahāvīragatatvena bhayam, yajñīyapaśuvasāsṛṅmāṃsādyālambanatayā varṇyamānā jugupsā ca rasābhāsāḥ/ vistṛtibhayāc cāmī nehodāhṛtāḥ sudhībhir unneyāḥ/
evam evānucitaviṣayā bhāvābhāsāḥ/
yathā--
sarve 'pi vismṛtipathaṃ viṣayāḥ prayātā
vidyāpi khedakalitā vimukhībabhūva/
sā kevalaṃ hariṇaśāvakalocanā me
naivāpayāti hṛdayād adhidevateva//
body.translated_text:
Here, when a certain woman coming from somewhere on a road, being followed by young men whose minds are captivated by her beauty and youth, at the time of her entering a house—when those [young men], eager for the boon of her command to follow [her] in order to know that their service is not fruitless, [she,] out of compassion born from remembering their extreme exertion, [gives] the command to follow—through the description of the <s>anubhāva</s> (consequent) in the form of casting about the garland of her lotus-eyes which communicates the giving of permission to follow, the <s>rati</s> (love) that is manifested, being understood through the plural as directed toward many objects, becomes a <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of <s>rasa</s>).
Or, for example—
"Seized in the cage of his arms, the newly-wed bride by the bridegroom trembles exceedingly, like a young doe caught in a net at that very moment." //
Here, because <s>rati</s> does not even slightly touch the new bride, it becomes a semblance through not being established in both parties (<s>anubhayaniṣṭha</s>).
As is stated—
"When <s>rati</s> is located in a subordinate hero (<s>upanāyaka</s>), when it is directed toward the wife of a sage or teacher, when it has many heroes as its object, and likewise when it is not established in both parties—" //
Here, the words 'sage' and 'teacher' are illustrative (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), so kings and others are also included.
Now, what is suggested here?—
"Humbly bent, restless, wide-open, utterly agitated—upon the sons of <s>Pāṇḍu</s>, the first glances of <s>Pāñcālī</s> (<s>Draupadī</s>) fall." //
Here, through the bent [glances], devotion toward <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s> prompted by his righteousness; through the restless [glances], alarm toward <s>Bhīmasena</s> prompted by his massive form; through the wide-open [glances], joy toward <s>Arjuna</s> prompted by hearing of his extraordinary valor; and through the utterly agitated [glances], eagerness toward <s>Nakula</s> and <s>Sahadeva</s> prompted by their supreme beauty—since these glances manifest <s>rati</s> of <s>Pāñcālī</s> directed toward many objects, it is only a <s>rasābhāsa</s>—thus say the modern [scholars]. The ancients, however, say that <s>rati</s> becomes a semblance when directed toward many heroes who are not [all] her husbands. In that case, just as with <s>Śṛṅgāra-rasa</s> itself, <s>Śṛṅgārābhāsa</s> (semblance of the erotic) is also twofold—from the distinction of union (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and separation (<s>vipralambha</s>). The semblance of union has just been illustrated above.
The semblance of separation, for example—
"He speaks incoherently for a moment, then falls silent the next; he casts upon every object a gaze without support; he draws long sighs; he holds not the slightest composure in his limbs—the lord of <s>Laṅkā</s> (<s>Rāvaṇa</s>), swallowed up by the loveliness of <s>Vaidehī</s> (<s>Sītā</s>)!" //
Here, this <s>vipralambha-rati</s> (love-in-separation) directed toward <s>Sītā</s> as its object, located in the lord of <s>Laṅkā</s>, has become a semblance through not being established in both parties and through being directed toward the wife of the world's teacher (<s>Rāma</s>); and the <s>unmāda</s> (madness), <s>śrama</s> (exhaustion), <s>moha</s> (delusion), <s>cintā</s> (anxiety), and <s>vyādhi</s> (sickness) manifested by the expressions 'speaks incoherently' and so on, having likewise become semblances, predominantly nourish [that <s>rati</s>] and constitute the ground for designating it as <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion). Similarly, <s>śoka</s> (grief) described as having a quarrelsome bad son and the like as its object, or as established in one who is passionless (<s>vītarāga</s>); <s>nirveda</s> (world-weariness) as located in a <s>Caṇḍāla</s> and others who are not qualified for <s>Brahmavidyā</s>; <s>krodha</s> (anger) and <s>utsāha</s> (enthusiasm) as located in a miser, coward, and the like, or as having one's father and the like as object; <s>vismaya</s> (wonder) as located in a conjurer and the like; <s>hāsa</s> (laughter) as having a teacher and the like as object; <s>bhaya</s> (fear) as located in a great hero; and <s>jugupsā</s> (disgust) described as having the fat, blood, and flesh of sacrificial animals as object—these are all <s>rasābhāsas</s>. Out of fear of prolixity, these have not been illustrated here; they are to be inferred by the learned.
In the same way, <s>bhāvābhāsas</s> (semblances of <s>bhāva</s>) are those directed toward inappropriate objects.
For example—
"All objects have departed to the path of oblivion; even learning, afflicted with weariness, has turned away; only she, the doe-eyed one, never departs from my heart, like a presiding deity." //

body.text: gurukule vidyābhyāsasamaye tadīyakanyālāvaṇyagṛhītamānasasyānyasya vā kasya cid apratiṣiddhagamanāṃ smarato deśāntaraṃ gatasyeyam uktiḥ/ atra ca svātmatyāgātyāgābhyāṃ srakcandanādiṣu viṣayeṣu, cirasevitāyāṃ vidyāyāṃ ca kṛtaghnatvam, asyāṃ ca lokottaratvam abhivyajyamānaṃ vyatirekavapuḥsmṛtim eva puṣṇātīti saiva pradhānam/ evaṃ ca tyāgābhāvagataṃ sārvadikatvaṃ vyañjayanty adhidevatopamāpi/ eṣā cānucitaviṣayakatvād anubhayaniṣṭhatvāc ca bhāvābhāsaḥ/ yadi punar iyaṃ tatpariṇetur evoktis tadā bhāvadhvanir eva//
body.translated_text: This is the utterance of someone in a <s>guru's</s> school (<s>gurukula</s>), during the time of studying, whose mind has been captivated by the beauty of the master's daughter—or of some other person who, remembering one to whom access is not forbidden, has gone to another country. Here, through both the renunciation and non-renunciation of oneself with respect to garlands, sandalwood, and other sensory objects, and in learning which was long cultivated, ingratitude is [suggested]; and in her, the extraordinary quality is manifested—this, taking the form of <s>smṛti</s> (memory) through contrast (<s>vyatireka</s>), is what is predominantly nourished.
